name: Kira Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Kira. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions or government. Everything today is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the stacker-reclaimer at the bauxite mine at Tallow Point. It's a huge machine on rails, longer than a football pitch, that builds the ore into long piles and then scoops it back out to load the trains. Most of the time I'm in a cab high up on the boom, watching the bucket wheel turn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a thinking job as much as a driving job, you're planning the piles so the trains get the right blend. What wears me out is the drive, fifty minutes each way, and the night shifts. At home Lars and I run thirty head of beef cattle on our forty hectares, and I use a chatbot every evening to keep the herd records and the books straight. That's my other job, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, it's a tool like any other. The market decides what's worth using, and it decided this was worth a bit, not a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's fine. I'd keep my job to sixty-two or so, and the cattle would tick along. I'd keep using the chatbot for the books because it saves me an hour a night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd keep working, keep the herd, and maybe buy a few more heifers in spring if the price is right. We'd keep our savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit like a dry year that turns out average.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does automation look like on your machine today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stacker already runs half on autopilot, it follows a programme and I correct it. There's talk of running it from the control room in town. I'd put my hand up for that tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using AI for the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Freya set it up two years ago when I was drowning in receipts. Now I talk to it about vaccination dates, feed costs, which steers to sell. Lars calls it my other husband.

S0.say: I'd say it's a tool like any other, and the market decided it was worth a bit, not a lot. I'd say it in a matter-of-fact way.
S0.think: Privately it's fine; I'd keep my job to about sixty-two and the cattle would tick along. I'd keep using the chatbot because it saves me an hour a night.
S0.do: Keeps working and running the herd as before. May buy a few more heifers in spring if the price is right and keeps savings where they are.
S0.feel: Calm, like a dry year that turns out average.
S0.quote: Lars calls it my other husband.
S0.fieldNote: Kira already uses AI daily, but for her small cattle business rather than the mine. Her free-market view frames AI as just another tool the market prices. Her machine is half automated already, and she would happily move to the town control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is how it's always been, and the people who move with it do fine. I wouldn't be crying about it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the stacker goes fully remote fast, and the cab I sit in becomes a museum piece. But I'm good with the software, so I reckon I'd be one of the ones they keep. And frankly, I'd like the shorter drive to the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the operations manager this month to put me on the control-room training first. I'd use AI to learn the scheduling side, which is where the real work goes. We'd also put a bit of savings into a better cattle-handling setup, so the farm can carry more of us later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. Maybe a bit pleased with myself, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Tallow Point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Henk on the other shift. He's a good operator but he doesn't want to learn the new screens. I'd try to show him, but you can't drag someone into the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the company should look after people like Henk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Offer them training, yes, and a fair package if they say no. But I don't think it's the company's job to keep a job going that's not needed. That's how businesses go broke and then nobody has a job.

S1.say: I'd say change is how it's always been and people who move with it do fine. I wouldn't be crying about it at the pub.
S1.think: Privately I think the stacker goes fully remote fast and my cab becomes a museum piece. I'm good with software, so I expect to be kept, and I'd like the shorter drive.
S1.do: Asks the operations manager this month for first place on control-room training and uses AI to learn the scheduling side. Puts some savings into better cattle-handling yards so the farm can carry more of their income later.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a bit pleased with herself.
S1.quote: You can't drag someone into the future.
S1.fieldNote: Kira expects to win under steady change, and she's frank about feeling a little smug. She supports training and fair packages but not keeping unneeded jobs alive, a clear free-market line. She is already shifting money towards the farm as a second base.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and families and communities need to pull together, not wait for the government to sort it. I'd tell young people to learn anything that keeps them useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one gets me. If AI runs the whole yard and plans the blend, there's no control room job for me either. I'd be sixty with about five months saved and a herd that pays for itself but not for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd push the herd up from thirty to fifty head while I still have a wage to borrow against, and use AI to plan the grazing tight. I'd cut the extras, no new truck and no trip to see Freya overseas. Once it arrives, the farm becomes the job, and Lars and I would sell direct to butchers and the local café my other daughter runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had something to grab onto. The cattle don't care about AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Borrowing to grow the herd just as your wage might end sounds risky. How do you think about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is risky, and I know it. But sitting still is risky too, it just feels safer. I'd rather owe the bank for cattle than have nothing to show at sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years of warning change for you, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm making the farm work on the fly, with no buffer. With longer, I could grow it slowly and pay as I go. The plan's the same, it's the speed that scares me.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shock and families and communities need to pull together rather than wait for the government. I'd tell young people to learn anything that keeps them useful.
S2.think: Privately this one gets me, because if AI runs the whole yard there's no control room job either. I'd be sixty with about five months saved and a herd that pays for itself but not for us.
S2.do: Grows the herd from thirty to fifty head straight away, borrowing against her wage, and plans grazing with AI. Cuts extras including a new vehicle and an overseas trip, then makes the farm the main income by selling direct to butchers and her daughter's café.
S2.feel: Anxious, but with something solid to hold onto in the cattle.
S2.quote: I'd rather owe the bank for cattle than have nothing to show at sixty.
S2.fieldNote: Kira's confidence drops in the two-year scenario, since her software skills no longer protect her. She responds by taking a deliberate risk on the farm and openly weighs it. Family and community, not government, are where she looks for support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you're willing to work. I'd be telling people at Tallow Point to get a second string to their bow now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three, past my sixty-two. I think I'd ride the control room job most of the way and grow the farm on the side. It's tight at the end but I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd get on the control-room training and grow the herd slowly, five or so head a year, paid from wages, not loans. I'd use AI to set up direct sales to the café and a couple of butchers. And I'd plan to stop at the mine at sixty-one if the farm's paying by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly it feels like a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Freya's a nurse in Norway, and I'd tell her to stay close to patients, people will want a human hand. Ingrid runs the café, and I'd tell her the same thing I tell myself: make it something people want to come to, not just somewhere to buy coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked a lot about the farm. What would you miss about the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew, and being up on the boom at sunrise. The pay, obviously. But not the drive and not the nights.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty if you're willing to work. I'd tell people at Tallow Point to get a second string to their bow now.
S3.think: Privately I'd ride the control room job most of the way to sixty-three and grow the farm on the side. It's tight at the end, but I'd be fine.
S3.do: Takes control-room training this year and grows the herd slowly from wages rather than loans. Uses AI to set up direct sales and plans to leave the mine at sixty-one if the farm is paying by then.
S3.feel: Uneasy at the back of her mind but mostly treating it as a project.
S3.quote: Make it something people want to come to, not just somewhere to buy coffee.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Kira's two-year gamble into a slow, debt-free plan. She leans on the farm and family business for her future and would leave the mine early once it pays. Her advice to her daughters is about the human side of their work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so there's no excuse for anyone not to plan. People should take responsibility for their own patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, I'd be sixty-eight and fully on the farm by then. It's mostly fine for me. I'd keep an eye on it because I'm curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to sixty-two, do the control-room move, and grow the herd steadily. I'd keep using AI for the books and probably for selling. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is a lot of springs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year version that could hurt the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots and AI make beef dirt cheap, or if everyone's eating something grown in a lab by then. I'd keep an eye on that. I don't know enough to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want governments to do with those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep apprenticeships going and keep taxes sensible so small farms and businesses can grow. Not big schemes. Let people stand on their own feet.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so there's no excuse not to plan. People should take responsibility for their own patch.
S4.think: Privately I'd be sixty-eight and fully on the farm by then, so it's mostly fine. I'd watch it out of curiosity.
S4.do: Works to sixty-two, moves to the control room and grows the herd steadily. Keeps using AI for the books and probably for sales.
S4.feel: Calm, because ten years is a lot of springs.
S4.quote: Ten years is a lot of springs.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years leaves Kira calm and planning a gradual shift to the farm. Her remaining worry is beef prices or lab-grown food, and she admits she doesn't know enough. Her wish list for government is small: apprenticeships and sensible taxes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be building the farm with no buffer. What would help is cheap loans for people setting up small businesses after the mine, and not a lot of red tape. Give me a fair chance and I'll do the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about how much people like me already use this stuff. The miners who'll be fine aren't the ones who know the machine best. They're the ones who've got something else going on.

headlineQuote: The miners who'll be fine aren't the ones who know the machine best. They're the ones who've got something else going on.
portrait: Kira Olsen is a 58-year-old stacker-reclaimer operator at the bauxite mine at Tallow Point, who also runs thirty head of beef cattle on forty hectares with her husband Lars and uses a chatbot every evening for the herd records and books. She believes in markets, self-reliance and family, and expects to move to the control room as the mine automates. She is calm on the plateau and under steady change, anxious if AGI arrives in two years and she has to make the farm her living with no buffer, and uneasy with five years. With ten years she is calm and plans a slow shift to the farm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd have to turn the farm into her main income in a hurry, with no buffer.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for people starting small businesses after the mine and little red tape.
